messages.subject: Re: Random intercepts in a picture naming experiment
messages.subject_clean: Random intercepts in a picture naming experiment
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone

(If it is not too late) I concur with Matt's response. My additional 
description is that items and the quantitative factors are somewhat
confounded. Ideally, you would want to have several items for each value 
of the factor(s) of interest.

In our paper on the same topic (Sadat et al. 2014; doi 
10.1016/j.cogpsych.2013.10.001), "we introduced [...] by-item random 
intercepts, and finally by-item random slopes for session" (because the 
same pictures appeared in each session). We thus faced the same 
limitations you point out.

Xavier

On 4/17/19 12:10 AM, Matt Goldrick wrote:
> Dear Hossein,
> 
> The magnitude of the picture intercepts should go down as your fixed 
> effects do a better job of capturing between-picture differences. But 
> it’s good to keep them to account for other factors that are not in your 
> fixed effects  (eg name agreement, picture complexity).
> 
> mg
> 
> On Tue, Apr 16, 2019 at 9:08 AM Hossein Karimi <karimihussein-Re5JQEeQqe8AvxtiuMwx3w at public.gmane.org 
> <mailto:karimihussein-Re5JQEeQqe8AvxtiuMwx3w at public.gmane.org>> wrote:
> 
>     Hi everyone,
> 
>     I'm analyzing data for picture naming experiment where we're looking
>     at the effects of Frequency and Phonological Neighborhood Density
>     (PND) on reaction times. I'm following Barr et al. (2013)'s
>     recommendation and trying to keep the random effects structure
>     maximal. I'm including random intercepts for subjects as well as
>     by-subjects random slopes for the all the predictors. However,  for
>     pictures, because a given picture has only one value for
>     frequency/PND, by-picture random slopes do not make sense.
> 
>     My questions is about including random /intercepts /for pictures. I
>     initially included them, but now I'm thinking a big part of why a
>     picture is hard/easy to name overall is because it's
>     frequent/infrequent or because it has a spare or dense PND. So, by
>     including random intercepts for pictures, I might be taking away
>     variance that would have otherwise been explained by the fixed
>     effects? Am I increasing the probability of making a Type II error,
>     by including intercepts for pictures?
> 
>     Thank you in advance for your help!
> 
>     Hossein
> 

-- 
F.-Xavier Alario
+33 4 13 55 09 72
https://lpc.univ-amu.fr/fr/profile/alario-francois-xavier
